classContent:
Today’s first class focused on getting everyone familiar with the class and comfortable speaking on stage.

Students began with self-introduction speeches, with a three-minute limit for Louis, Kenny, Kailyn, and Winston, and a five-minute limit for Jennifer.

We then introduced the basics of Original Oratory: choosing a personal perspective, developing ideas, and organizing them into a clear speech. Using the glacier collapse and resulting mudslides as a reference point, students practised sharing their own ideas through impromptu speeches.

The main focus today was self-awareness. At this stage, we are less concerned with polished results and more interested in helping students recognize what they did well, assess what needs improvement, and choose something specific to practise.

homework.title: Your perspective on the glacier event
steps:
Develop the impromptu speech from class into a written speech of approximately 200–400 words. Use the glacier event as a starting point and expand the personal perspective chosen in class.

Students should:

- Organize the speech with a clear beginning, middle, and ending.
- Explain their ideas more fully through reasons, examples, or personal experiences.
- Use transitions such as “first,” “second,” and “finally” where appropriate.
- Develop and express their ideas in their own words.
- Practise the completed speech aloud once or twice.

Preparation expectation

Homework means preparing to give a presentation at the beginning of the next class. Writing is one part of the process; practising aloud helps students check the flow, notice unclear sections, and become more familiar with their message.

Every class will begin with student presentations. These opening speeches will provide the main basis for feedback shared with parents, with additional observations from classroom behavior and participation. A little preparation will help students apply their feedback and show their progress.
homework.prepareFor: Be ready to present at the beginning of the next class.

classContent:
We began by checking the previous homework. Preparation was not yet consistent across the group, so we moved on rather than holding the planned homework presentations.

Students started with impromptu speaking, received individual feedback, and practised organizing their responses through answer, reason, example, and message. We emphasized that the final message should offer something useful to listeners, such as a concrete action or an idea they can apply in their own lives.

We then introduced cause, effect, impact, and solution using more than ten articles about events from the past week. In a group presentation format, students practised summarizing the content and developing their own ideas: what happened, why it happened, its wider impact on society, and possible solutions.

This was an introductory exercise in organizing an original response to current events. We will continue developing these skills, but our main priority remains strengthening the foundations of public speaking, including clear delivery, purposeful gestures, focused content, and audience connection.

homework.title: AI surveillance and the distribution of power
steps:
Prepare a speech based on Story 18: AI Surveillance and Distribution of Power, which we reviewed together in class.

Students should write approximately 300–500 words, where possible, covering the causes, immediate effects, wider social impact, and potential solutions. They should be ready to deliver it next class.

Note cards with keywords and an outline are welcome. Students should practise explaining their ideas to the audience rather than reading the full speech directly from paper.
homework.prepareFor: Be ready to deliver the speech at the next class.

classContent:
1. Warm-up: Reliance on AI in important decisions  
Students responded to:

“What’s your opinion on relying on AI, especially for things that matter?”

The teacher supplied discussion material about economic dependence on AI growth, expectations for employees and government officials to use AI to improve efficiency, and the potential consequences of using inaccurate AI analysis in sensitive international decisions.

2. Response structure  
Students organized their answers using:

Opinion → Reason → Supporting evidence, example, or hypothetical situation → Impact

The focus was on stating a clear position, explaining why, developing specific support, and showing why the issue matters. Hypothetical examples should be clearly identified as imagined situations.

3. Homework presentations and delivery practice  
Students presented their prepared speeches, with feedback on vocal strength, pacing, purposeful pauses, emotional expression, specific language, and audience connection. They also practised making the main message simpler and more memorable through emphasis and repetition. Winston’s presentation included an additional Q&A.

➜ Additional class content — Original Oratory brainstorming:  
Students brainstormed ideas for their Original Oratory speeches: 10 minutes for Jennifer and 5 minutes for everyone else. We discussed choosing topics with a personal connection and a meaningful societal impact, while making sure each topic is distinctive and researchable.

For the personal connection, students worked on establishing why they care and showing relevant experience or credibility. We also explored pathos—emotional appeal: using emotional language together with a story to help the audience connect with the speaker’s feelings.

homework.title: Develop ten Original Oratory topics
steps:
Develop the 10 topics with a little more descriptive detail, then prepare to share them with the teacher. For each topic, consider:

➜ Personal connection: Why do you care? What experience or perspective connects you to it?
➜ Societal impact: Who does it affect, and why does it matter?
➜ Uniqueness: What specific angle makes your approach distinctive?
➜ Researchability: Can you find credible information to support and develop it?

When explaining the personal connection, use specific details and, where relevant, a short story to help the audience understand both your experience and your emotions.
homework.prepareFor: Prepare to share your developed topics with the teacher.

classContent:
Students shared their opinions about the Tesla Roadster. Feedback focused on a clear opinion, supporting points and detail, and a message at the end.

Today’s main purpose was to introduce the WSDA impromptu speech competition. We briefly introduced different prompt types: analogies, hypothetical situations, quotations, direct questions, and single words. Students tried several practice activities and received a worksheet with a printed speech structure to practise. We also worked through how to answer a single-word prompt using “blueberry.”

homework.title: Quotation prompt worksheet
steps: Complete the worksheet for the quotation prompt beginning “Silence can…”, then prepare to present your response next class.
homework.prepareFor: Present your response next class.

classContent:
◆ Personal perspective and persuasion: We focused on sharing a personal perspective using ethos, pathos and logos, then giving supporting details. Students used one of the speech structures to develop their perspective into a speech.

◆ AI and energy discussion: The class prompt asked students to imagine a world where we never have enough energy to support ourselves, while we are in a race to improve AI, which requires a great deal of power: ‘What do you think we should do?’ Discussion directions on the slide included creating more energy, slowing down AI, finding efficient ways to solve the problem, improving technology and creating a consensus. These were ideas to consider, rather than a single prescribed answer.

◆ Organizing the speech: Students could use Cause → Effect → Impact → Solution, or the simpler structure Answer → Reason → Example → Message. The focus was to share a perspective, develop it with supporting details, and use one of these structures to create a speech.

Today’s first lesson covered the foundations of public speaking through discussion, speech analysis, and practical exercises. We focused on both developing ideas and becoming more comfortable presenting on stage.

Understanding public-speaking fears: We discussed fear of the stage and fear of the content—feeling nervous in front of others and feeling unsure about what to say. Repeated speaking practice helped students begin building comfort with both.

Building self-awareness: We explored our eyes, feet, hands, facial expressions, and emotions, and how these affect what an audience experiences. Students practised paying attention to their posture, gestures, expression, and delivery.

Articulation and emotional expression: We practised speaking clearly and communicating different emotions. We also explored a bigger, more powerful character voice to encourage projection and a stronger stage presence. Maintaining energy throughout a speech, rather than letting the voice fade, was an important coaching point.

Learning from a world champion speech: We watched and discussed a world champion’s presentation, looking at gestures, strong emotions, personal storytelling, humor, pauses, and confident delivery. Students considered how these choices make a speech more engaging.

Impromptu speaking structures: We introduced several ways to organise an unprepared response and had students practise using one. Answers were often short, so our next focus is developing each idea more fully and making better use of speaking time.

Adding specific details: We worked on moving beyond simply listing facts about ourselves. Explaining when an interest began, what we learned, and what we hope to do next gives the audience a clearer picture and helps turn a brief answer into a fuller speech.

homework.title: A self-introduction with specific details
steps:
Prepare a self-introduction speech using this structure:

- My name
- One thing about me
- When did I start?
- What did I learn?
- What do I want to do in the future?

Choose one thing about yourself and develop it through the three supporting parts. Include specific details and examples instead of only naming an interest or activity.

Homework means preparing to present in the next class, not just completing the writing. Please practise the speech aloud at least two or three times to feel more warmed up and comfortable stepping on stage.
homework.prepareFor: Prepare to present in the next class.

classContent: This class was cancelled.

Students reviewed self-introductions, answered warm-up impromptu questions, and received initial feedback. They then worked on foundational speaking skills from the PowerPoint.

➜ Specific details: Replace vague words such as “things” and “stuff” with precise descriptions.
➜ The bigger idea: Take a step back and consider the broader point behind the answer.
➜ Define the message: Make the takeaway clear—the message gives the speech value.
➜ Filtering: Select the ideas and details that best support the message.

➜ Speaking structures shown:
→ Answer → Reason → Example → Message
→ CARE: Connect → Answer → Reason → Example
→ PREP: Point → Reason → Example → Point
→ OREO: Opinion → Reason → Example → Opinion

Everyone was asked to write down three things they would like to do with an extra free hour each day, numbered 1, 2, and 3, on paper or in a notebook. This exercise helps students generate ideas before organizing a spoken response.

Articulation and emotional-transference drills were planned for the final section; completion has not yet been confirmed.

homework.title: Two impromptu questions
steps:
Prepare answers to both questions using Answer → Reason → Example → Message:

1. Do you want to be Spider-Man or Spider-Woman?
2. What would you do if you never ran out of money?

Give a direct answer, explain why, add a specific example, and finish with a clear takeaway for the audience.
homework.prepareFor: Prepare answers using Answer → Reason → Example → Message.

classContent:
Students shared their thoughts about the Tesla Roadster and its recently introduced features. Feedback included developing a clear message and practising confident delivery, word emphasis, audience eye contact, steady pacing, and awareness of arm movements.

We also worked on a seven-minute impromptu speech.

homework.title: Impromptu speaking worksheet and practice
steps:
Practise two or three impromptu questions. Complete the worksheet for the question assigned in class. If you cannot remember that question, you can use a new one:

“What kind of innovations do you think you’ll see in 2030?”
homework.prepareFor: Practise two or three impromptu questions and complete the worksheet.

classContent:
For our first class, we had two students returning from summer camp and two completely new students. The lesson gave everyone an opportunity to settle in and helped us understand their starting points in confidence, delivery, and speech organization.

We began with voice and body warm-up games, followed by articulation practice. Students then worked on self-introductions before moving into impromptu speaking, focusing on answering questions directly and organizing their reasons. The warm-up question was: “If you suddenly found a wallet containing RMB 10,000, what would you do? Would you spend it, give it to the police, or handle it another way?” This also led to a discussion about choosing language and ideas appropriate for an audience.

Later, we discussed a recent glacier-related flooding event involving Nepal and China. Students explored a current event in more depth, discussed the importance of being careful as the climate and world around us change, and practised delivering a short, organized speech.

homework.title: Self-introduction or glacier speech
steps: Students can prepare a self-introduction speech, practise the printed glacier speech, or work on both. They should be ready to deliver their chosen speech next class, focusing on clear organization, an audible voice throughout, and their individual practice points below.
homework.prepareFor: Prepare to deliver your selected speech at the next class.

classContent:
Students reviewed the two earlier homework options: a self-introduction and the printed glacier speech. The self-introduction focused on one main interest, with supporting details about when it began, what the speaker learned, and a future goal, followed by a return to the main point.

Students were encouraged to present what they remembered instead of relying on reading the full script. Stacey and Liam both demonstrated complete memorized presentations in their second attempts, correcting the earlier impression that the prepared speeches had not been shown. Tongtong also came up and spoke successfully after further encouragement. The lesson emphasized that students can begin, continue through small mistakes, and participate even when some vocabulary is unfamiliar.

The lesson began with warm-up activities and a review of homework. Students warmed up their voices, articulation and bodies, then focused on adding hand gestures and organizing ideas with “first,” “second” and “finally.” They practised an impromptu speech, trying to apply the feedback they had received.

Finally, students brainstormed and began crafting their next speech: “If I could have a dream robot.” They considered what their robot would do and what it would be capable of.

Preparation and attendance: Tongtong, Stacey and Liam had all memorized their previous speeches, which was a welcome surprise. This was Emily’s first class, so the previous homework requirement did not apply to her. Tianyou was absent, which is why no individual speaking feedback was recorded for this session.

homework.title: If I could have a dream robot
steps: Use the printed worksheet to develop your dream-robot speech: What would your robot do? What would it be capable of?
Try to complete the worksheet, memorize your speech, and present it in the next class.
homework.prepareFor: Present your dream-robot speech in the next class.

classContent:
We began by reviewing the homework speeches. Students practised presenting with a voice loud enough for the audience to hear clearly.

We then introduced structures for answering impromptu questions, helping students organize an answer, explain their reasoning, and support their ideas with an example. The frameworks described were:

◆ PREP: Point, Reason, Example, Point.  
◆ OREO: Opinion, Reason, Example, Opinion.  
◆ Answer, Reason, Example, Message.  
◆ CREI: Claim, Reasoning, Example, Impact.  
◆ Connect, Answer, Reasoning, Example.

Students worked through four examples. They wrote out the first two answers to become comfortable with the structure and logic. They then practised answering without preparation, trying to follow PREP while speaking.

homework.title: Impromptu speaking practice
steps:
Complete the last two written examples, using the structures introduced in class to organize the answers.

If possible, also practise the short dialogue between the bank robber and the security guard.
homework.prepareFor: Complete the last two written examples; optionally practise the dialogue.

classContent: We did a little impromptu speaking practice. The focus was to organize responses using Answer–Reason–Example–Message (AREM): answer the question, give a reason, add an example, and finish with a message.

homework.title: AREM impromptu speaking practice
steps:
Practise answering impromptu questions a bit more using Answer–Reason–Example–Message (AREM). Answer the question, give a reason, add an example, and finish with a message.

Use these five questions for practice:

1. How has technology helped you in your life?
2. Should we remove electric bikes? Think about Shanghai.
3. What would you do in a world that is submerged in water?
4. What would the world be like without any trees?
5. What do you think about flying cars?
homework.prepareFor: Practise organizing impromptu answers with Answer–Reason–Example–Message.

classContent:
◆ Impromptu speaking and class focus: Stacey and Liam focused mainly on impromptu speaking. I felt this was a competition area they could enter. There have also been some student switches, so introducing a large amount of new material could be difficult for different students.

◆ Thinking, logic and speaking length: The aim was to strengthen critical thinking and the ability to organize logic and structure, while gradually increasing answers from around 30 seconds toward eventually two minutes. This would help prepare them for other competition opportunities, including TOC impromptu, the recently upgraded WSDA impromptu work mentioned in class, ESTP and similar competitions. These were preparation goals, not a claim that the students already spoke for two minutes or that they had entered a competition.

◆ Developing answers: We focused on building an argument and organizing it with Answer → Reason → Example → Message. We continued exploring ways to develop the logic of answers and speak for longer, with more practice questions to work on. Stacey needed to expand her short answers, while Liam needed to slow down and give more thorough answers.

Students practised self-introductions, answered follow-up questions, and delivered a second attempt using a clear speech structure. We focused on developing specific details so the audience could learn more about each speaker’s interests and experiences.

The structure was: “One thing about me is...,” “I started when...,” “What I learned was...,” and “In the future, I want to...,” followed by a conclusion returning to the main idea. We discussed how repeating the main point at the end helps listeners remember it.

At this stage, students are learning to feel comfortable speaking more and expanding their answers. As their confidence develops, they will also need to select and organize their content within a time limit. Individual delivery work included voice projection, pacing, pauses, gestures, and awareness of hands and feet on stage. As students become comfortable, they may be able to speak for three, five, or even ten minutes. For competitions and other timed presentations, they will then need to select what to keep and guide the speech toward its main point: first learning to say more, then learning to say it within a limit.

homework.title: Write and rehearse your self-introduction
steps: Introduce your name and one thing about yourself. Develop three supporting parts: when you started, what you learned, and what you would like to do in the future.
If possible, aim to write at least around 200 words. Use the writing process to organize your thoughts, logic and structure, rather than simply putting words on paper.
Practise and memorize the speech so you can deliver it in the next class. Aim for two minutes; one minute and thirty seconds is also acceptable.
Make sure you complete the task. If possible, send a video showing your completed speech.
homework.prepareFor: Deliver your memorized self-introduction in the next class.

classContent:
We began with voice and body warm-ups, followed by articulation practice. Students then reviewed and presented their self-introductions, with Jarvis speaking first. Feedback focused on controlling distracting hand movements, remembering prepared material, and connecting ideas logically so the audience could follow.

We then explored food waste in school cafeterias: the current problem, possible solutions, what some other schools are doing, and what students could choose to do themselves to reduce waste.

Students used a small amount of supplied evidence and information to develop their own opinions. They practised organizing and explaining their points with transitions such as “First,” “Second,” and “Finally.” The lesson included writing and presenting their topic-based speeches, with feedback on logic, detail, pronunciation, pauses, and delivery.

Completing homework at home is only part of the task. Students also need to prepare so they can present it in class, remembering what they intend to say or at least knowing their main ideas and their order. Written preparation helps students develop structure, logic, and specific details. Speaking practice helps them become comfortable communicating those ideas aloud. The aim is familiarity with the content, rather than reproducing every sentence perfectly. Students can use their own words: there is no single correct wording when sharing their own ideas.

homework.title: Food-waste speech
steps: Write out the food-waste speech and practise it aloud at home, ready to present next class. Organize the information and personal opinions clearly, use transitions, and explain the proposed actions for reducing waste.

Jarvis and Owen particularly need to complete the written work: the teacher felt they had not written their speeches during the activity. Elsa and Pinkie did not complete the previous homework, so completing this assignment was specifically emphasized. Their later writing and presentation efforts in class remain part of their positive progress.
homework.prepareFor: Present your food-waste speech next class.

classContent:
◆ Student presentations and feedback:
Students presented their prepared speeches or personal experiences. The main coaching points were:
→ Organize ideas so the audience can follow the story.
→ Connect an experience to a clear message, rather than only describing what happened.
→ Finish with a meaningful takeaway or an appropriate call to action.
→ Remove repeated words and unnecessary details.
→ Use pauses instead of filling every silence.
→ Give classmates attention and keep the recording area still while they speak.
Jarvis and Owen spoke about their National Day holidays. Elsa shared her LEGOLAND experience. Remy’s topic wasn’t specified in the recovered notes.
◆ Articulation: making each sound clear:
The lesson focused on opening the mouth and finishing sounds so words are easy to understand. The tongue twisters were:
→ Sixty silly skeletons.
→ Which witch is which?
→ Sandy sells seashells by the seashore.
→ Truly rural, truly rural, truly rural, truly rural.
The practice sequence was to start slowly, repeat each line three times, then increase speed without losing clarity.
◆ The four Ps of vocal variety:
   - Pitch: a high or low voice, such as a squeaky bee and a deep bear.
   - Power: a louder or softer voice, such as “STOP!” compared with “Psst…”
   - Pace: speaking quickly or slowly to suit the meaning.
   - Pause: stopping deliberately to give listeners time or create anticipation, such as “I have… a surprise!”
◆ Character voices and role-play:
The Bear and the Bee dialogue gave students two contrasting characters: a hungry bear trying to get honey and a bee reluctant to share it. The aim was to make their voices and intentions sound different, then switch roles.
Two additional scenes were:
→ The banana robber: a robber brings a banana instead of a gun. The guard says, “Hey, hands up!” and the robber replies, “But do you want a banana?”
→ The watermelon seller: a buyer wants juice, but the seller only sells whole watermelons. Students use their voices to show the characters’ different attitudes.
◆ Emphasis and expression:
Using “I want watermelon juice,” students explored how stressing a different word changes the meaning:
→ I: who wants it?
→ Want: how strongly do I want it?
→ Watermelon: which kind?
→ Juice: a drink rather than the whole fruit?
Another exercise used “I’m so hungry!” with four different deliveries: excited, secretive, angry and exhausted.
The performance checklist was clear sounds, a distinct character voice, an emphasized word, and purposeful use of the four Ps.
◆ Robot faces, voices and emotions:
The extension asked whether a robot can show a feeling and what we notice in its face, voice and body.
Students distinguished observations from guesses:
→ “I notice…” describes something visible or audible.
→ “My guess is…” explains an interpretation.
A robot can use cameras and microphones to collect information, software to choose actions, motors to move its face and speakers to produce a voice. The lesson included a real robot lip-sync demonstration.
The central discussion point is that a smile or cheerful voice can communicate an emotion, but does not by itself establish what is felt inside.
The final creative prompt was to perform a kind robot greeting—“Hello. Would you like help?”—using one facial movement and one voice change.

homework.title: AI, emotions and our lives
steps: Write out a speech presenting your personal opinions and thoughts on whether AI can have emotions and why emotions are important in our lives.
Include an opening, body and conclusion.
Use “first,” “second” and “finally” to organize your ideas.
homework.prepareFor: A written speech explaining your personal opinions on AI and emotions.

classContent:
We started with homework presentations and then moved into the main class topic: why do we do things that are dangerous even though we know they may be bad for us? We mainly talked about roller coasters, using the recent situation discussed around Six Flags in the U.S. as the starting point. Students then tried to express their ideas, using a simple speech structure and relating the question to their own lives: describe one situation you saw or something you did; ask why people do it; explain how it affects themselves or others; and consider what we can do. The aim was to identify one aspect of our own lives where we do this ourselves and go deeper into the question, rather than only talking about roller coasters. This discussion and expression practice was the main activity.

I also raised a question about the direction of the class: if only one student completes the homework, could we consider moving toward impromptu speaking instead, with less emphasis on homework? For prepared speaking, students need to practise preparing a speech and then presenting it. Without that preparation, it will be very hard for them to learn those skills. This is a possible direction to consider, not a confirmed change.

Roller-coaster discussion: people like the crazy speed and quick turns. They want to go again and again, and want faster and faster rides. Why? The experience is exciting and unique, and some people want to show off. We used the recent Six Flags situation mentioned in class as a news starting point. The slide raised concerns about rides breaking apart, derailments, brain problems, broken bones, vomiting and dizziness; these were discussion and research points, not independently verified claims about a particular incident. The question was: do you want more dangerous rides because they are fun, even if they increase the chance of injury or death? What should we do?

Personal connection and structure: choose one situation you saw or something you did. Why do people do this? How does it affect themselves or others? What can we do? The aim is to connect the outside-world example with a personal instance, ask ourselves the deeper question, and offer a solution.

homework.title: Combine and polish the two in-class speech parts
steps: Combine the two parts we worked on in class into one speech, then think about how to polish it. Would you change any words? Would you add more description to your stories? The first part is the roller-coaster situation—the input we got from world news. The second part is the output and the audience connection: a personal instance that has happened, leading us deeper into the question, “Why do we do this?”, and then offering a solution. You already have the basis for both parts. Bring them together and polish them, like working from a rough draft, so you can present in the next class. You do not need to memorize the speech at this point, but I expect everyone to finish the homework.
homework.prepareFor: Present in the next class. Memorization is not required at this stage; completing the homework is expected.

classContent:
◆ Prepared speeches and topic focus: Students spoke about why people have the habit of doing dangerous things. Many focused on the roller-coaster situation, but the aim was to include dangerous things people do in their own lives and explain why they do them, rather than repeatedly focus on death. The personal example belonged in the speech they were supposed to prepare; this was not a request to give a new personal example immediately during the discussion.

◆ Organizing before speaking: Students could use time before class, including when they arrived early, or while other students were speaking to write and organize ideas in their notebooks. They could put those notes on the table in front of them and use them while speaking. Writing ideas down becomes especially helpful as the content and information become more difficult.

◆ Persuasive speaking: We went over ethos, pathos and logos. Ethos builds credibility through our stories; pathos persuades through emotions; logos uses logic, statistics, studies and facts. We considered how these approaches help establish why a message matters and encourage an audience to do something.

◆ Worked example—exercise and diet: The slides used persuading people that losing weight through exercise and diet is important as an example. We connected ethos with telling a story, pathos with how it feels, and logos with discussing health risks. The example listed heart attack, cancer, stroke, diabetes and death in connection with obesity. These were classroom examples of persuasive content.

◆ Agree or disagree—‘People should go to spas’: We also used this statement to consider an agreeing or disagreeing position and how ethos, pathos and logos could support that position.

homework.title: Ethos: a winter story
steps: Share a short story about what you do in winter.
homework.prepareFor: Complete the worksheet’s ethos task.

classContent:
Today we worked on self-introductions, voice and body-language warm-ups, and an introduction to impromptu speech structure. During the superpower impromptu activity, students found it difficult to develop and express their own answers. Some were hesitant to share, so I provided speaking content to help them participate and practise the structure.

This does not mean they lack the ability to create their own speeches. They need more time and guided practice to develop their ideas and become comfortable expressing them. We will gradually reduce their reliance on paper, while continuing to use notes when needed. The priority is making sure they can form and communicate their own thoughts before expecting them to speak entirely without support.

homework.title: Write your own self-introduction
steps: Students should write their own self-introduction and prepare to deliver it next class. Ideally, they should practise enough to present from memory without looking at the paper. Parents can help by asking questions, listening, and encouraging rehearsal, while allowing the ideas and wording to remain the student’s own. A simple introduction they have written and understand is a useful starting point.
homework.prepareFor: Present your self-introduction at the next class.

classContent:
The lesson focused on preparing Richard, Luna, and Molly for their Tuesday speeches. Richard and Luna were preparing to compete, while Molly was trying to take part. The students had not completed their previous homework, and this session focused on their competition preparation.

Richard and Luna brought their speeches, which I helped edit and adjust. I helped Molly create a speech based on what she would like to do. All three received help with their content as well as their presentation, with the aim of improving as much as possible before Tuesday.

We practised pronunciation, articulation, and enunciation to make the words clearer. Each student also worked on hand gestures and body language alongside their speech. Attention and focus exercises included practising how to manage distractions and stay focused while presenting. The lesson brought these speaking skills together in a short preparation period: developing the content, expressing it clearly, and supporting it with gestures and physical presentation.

At the time, the instruction was to prepare according to the school’s requirements. I did not yet know that the event was UCDP. The later clarification was a speech of 60–90 seconds; this was not a duration already known during the lesson.

homework.title: Practise the competition speech for Tuesday
steps: Practise the edited or newly created speech according to the school’s requirements, ready for Tuesday’s presentation. Rehearse it several times rather than only having the written speech ready.

Include the pronunciation, articulation, and enunciation practised in class. Rehearse the hand gestures and body language for the speech, and practise maintaining attention and focus when there are distractions. Repeated practice and preparation could help make the Tuesday presentation stronger.
homework.prepareFor: Tuesday’s presentation, following the school’s requirements.
homework.note:
Later clarification: the event was UCDP, with a speech lasting 60–90 seconds. These details became known after the lesson.

The teacher also extended the rehearsal instruction to a student who was not there.

classContent:
Students presented self-introductions or prepared speeches and received feedback on detail, preparation, voice projection, audience contact, vocal variation, and pauses. Repeated speaking attempts gave opportunities to practise the feedback. The group seemed a little shy; the teacher asked how many students already knew one another.

We practised pausing together using Molly’s ice-skating speech: “Hello, everyone”—pause—“My name is Molly”—pause—“I love ice skating.” Claps marked sentence endings and natural breaks so students could hear and feel where to stop, rather than speaking continuously. Students could then replace the claps with silent pauses.

The practice passage described moving across the ice and feeling the cold air, and how skating can be fun but also hard. It referred to an ice-skating event in Shenzhen in September and skaters showing their moves. It then developed the message that learning one push, turn, or step at a time—and getting up after falling—helps small efforts lead to bigger achievements: “Every small try helps me get better. Small steps today can help me do big things tomorrow.” These were elements of the practice speech. The teacher also recalled advice from a public-speaking champion about deliberately counting pauses in a speech.

Students then began writing down speaking frameworks:

◆ PREP: introduced through Point, Reason, and Example as the simplest starting structure.
◆ OREO: Opinion, Reason, Example, Opinion.
◆ CARE: Connect, Answer, Reason, Example. “Connect” means first reaching out to the audience; the teacher modelled this by asking, “How many of you are hungry?” before moving into the answer.
◆ ARM: introduced with emphasis on ending with a message—what the speaker wants to tell the audience.
◆ CREI: introduced as a related debate framework, with similarities to the other structures.

Students who needed more writing support were asked to copy the first framework; stronger writers could copy more. Practice with these structures was planned after the break; its completion has not yet been reported.

classContent:
◆ What we did: First we warmed up our voices and bodies. Then we went over “AI should replace all teachers at school.” We watched a short video about a U.S. school described as already doing this since 2014, and how it had progressed and continued with that approach.

◆ Testing the arguments: We went through different points and reasoning for both sides to test the strength of the students' ideas and their ability to respond. For rebuttal, we mainly talked through why the points might be wrong on both sides. Then each student practised saying an opening statement for their side. The discussion was there to give both sides more ammunition—more information they could use to improve what they were saying. We want them to listen, understand the topic more thoroughly, and go deeper into their points.

◆ Detailed activity notes and coaching

We began with voice and body warm-ups, then explored the debate motion “AI should replace all teachers at school.” We watched a short video presenting a U.S. school described as using this approach since 2014, and discussed how the approach had developed.

We examined points and reasoning for both sides and tested how students could respond to challenges. The rebuttal activity was an oral discussion of why each side’s arguments might be wrong. Each student then practised an opening statement for their side, checking the strength of their ideas and developing a more thorough understanding of the motion.

We returned to the previous stakeholder task: identify who a technology affects, explain how it affects each group, and explain why those people should care. Opening responses and speeches highlighted the need to connect these effects into a clear line of reasoning rather than only describe the technology.

Content coaching covered developing students’ own ideas, using transition words, and focusing on three main points that can each be explored in more depth. We distinguished writing a speech and reading it aloud from presenting the ideas to listeners.

Delivery coaching covered purposeful pauses when using a script and engaging the people in the room. Although the class was being filmed, the recording camera was not the audience. Eye contact, addressing a listener by name, purposeful gestures, and expressive changes in volume or tone were discussed as ways to engage listeners once the content becomes familiar.

James’s 49-second impromptu response prompted coaching on developing fuller explanations toward one minute, one minute and 30 seconds, or two minutes. Three minutes was the upper limit discussed for expository-style competition preparation.

We then held a small debate: James and Charles formed one team, and Berlingo and Yiyi formed the other. Before the debate responses, the teacher examined both teams’ points and explained where those points could be challenged. This discussion supplied further information students could use to revise and strengthen their arguments. The feedback emphasized clear structure, relevant personal examples, listening carefully, incorporating new information, selecting precise linking words, and developing deeper explanations.

◆ Staying on the point: A major focus was staying on task—arguing against the actual point being made, rather than moving to other points. Students needed to listen carefully and identify exactly what each side was saying so their rebuttal addressed it directly.

classContent:
Students began with a debate warm-up discussing whether AI-generated pictures could be considered “normal.” They practised stating a position, supporting it with evidence and examples, and organizing their responses so listeners could follow each argument. Feedback was shared between turns, giving students opportunities to apply the guidance they heard.

The main speaking and reasoning skills were:

◆ Clear transitions: Introduce arguments with phrases such as “My first contention,” “My first argument,” or “My first point.” These signposts help judges and the opposing side follow the case, especially at faster debate speeds.
◆ Evidence and explanation: Give specific examples, explain what they demonstrate, and connect them to the argument. With no time limit for this exercise, students were encouraged to develop their reasoning fully.
◆ Impact and comparison: Explain who is affected, why the outcome matters, and why their side’s position produces a stronger outcome than the alternative.
◆ Conviction and delivery: Use firm, respectful statements, purposeful emphasis, clear articulation, and pauses that allow important points to register.
◆ Conclusions: Bring the arguments together and finish with a clear statement of the position and its significance.

Students then took part in mini debates: April versus Arthur, followed by Audrey versus Teresa and Ning. This gave them an opportunity to apply the earlier speaking guidance in an opposing-side format.

We also explored “Students should be able to grade their own teachers.” The discussion considered the perspectives of students, parents, teachers, principals, and education boards. Potential benefits included useful feedback for improvement, students raising concerns about safety, and better support for students. Possible concerns included retaliatory or false feedback, popularity and voting dynamics, differing perspectives, discrimination, and judging teachers before having sufficient information. These ideas provided a basis for considering competing interests and comparing the consequences of each side’s arguments.

The mini debates highlighted a shared priority: state a clear claim, identify the opponent’s claim accurately, and explain the disagreement. When both sides’ points remain unclear, the exchange becomes harder to follow and can turn into repeated assertions rather than a developing argument.

classContent:
◆ Warm-up: First, everyone went through three possible topics: whether AI extinction is overexaggerated compared with other potential catastrophes; whether a person on death row should be executed again if the first execution failed; and whether public executions should be broadcast live. For the AI topic, we considered other problems such as a potential plague and its fallout, food-related problems and obesity, and nuclear catastrophe. Everyone shared their own thoughts, opinions and reasons. We tried to go through CREI—claim, reasoning, evidence or example, and impact—to fully develop the answers.

◆ Mini debate: In the second half, we kept things a little lighter after the students had just finished their national competition. It was four students versus Coach Kai, working together as a team to try to overturn my impromptu answers. The motion was “Men should wear makeup.” One of the biggest problems I noticed was that students could easily stray off topic. We need to stay with the question, go deeper, and support the points we've expressed. A reason on its own isn't always enough: give evidence, examples or potential scenarios that show what you mean.

◆ Detailed activity notes and coaching

The class began with three warm-up discussion topics:

1. Is the risk of AI causing human extinction exaggerated compared with other potential catastrophes?
2. Should a person sentenced to death face another execution attempt if they survive the first?
3. Should public executions be broadcast live?

Students shared their own thoughts, opinions and reasons on the three warm-up topics. The AI-risk discussion considered other possible problems and catastrophes, including epidemics and their consequences, food-related problems and obesity, and nuclear catastrophe. Students practised developing their answers with CREI: a claim, reasoning, evidence or an example, and an explanation of impact.

Ning was the first speaker. Feedback focused on presenting to the audience even when using a script: projecting a loud, clear voice, looking at listeners when possible, and speaking directly to the people in the room. Structure coaching covered transition words and complete transition sentences, including “first,” “second,” and “finally,” to identify the purpose of each part of an argument. Students were encouraged to explain potential social impacts with clear examples.

Audrey’s response lasted 1 minute and 13 seconds. Further coaching covered introducing the topic before the main points and developing those points using the CREA framework discussed in class, with reasoning, evidence or an example, and an explanation of impact where possible. She was also encouraged to use her preparation time more fully and speak with greater conviction.

April spoke on whether a person sentenced to death should face another execution attempt if the first one fails. Her feedback emphasized introducing the topic before presenting arguments, using transition sentences such as “My first reason,” “My first argument,” “My first contention,” or “My first claim,” and ending with a summary of the main position and reasons. An introduction provides necessary context for the audience, while a closing summary gives the speech a clear finish.

Teresa spoke last, for more than two minutes—approximately 2 minutes and 13 seconds. Her feedback recognized two effective examples, the topic’s connection with the audience, fully developed ideas, and a well-prepared, coherent presentation.

In the second half, the four students worked together as one team in a mini debate against Coach Kai. They tried to challenge and overturn the coach’s impromptu answers, keeping the session lighter after the holiday break. A shared area to improve was staying on topic: arguments sometimes moved away from the question instead of developing the stated points more deeply. Students need to connect supporting evidence, examples and possible scenarios directly to their claims, rather than stop after giving a reason.

The mini-debate motion was “Men should wear makeup.” Teresa, April, Audrey and Ning spoke for the pro side in that order, while Coach Kai spoke for the con side. This was a separate activity from the warm-up round, where Ning spoke first and Teresa spoke last.

The students presented concrete, varied examples: cultural traditions, stage performances, professional practice, covering an actor’s tattoo, and personal confidence. Teresa introduced culture, performances and confidence, and Ning returned to those themes in the closing. The tattoo example explained a specific situation in which makeup could solve a practical problem. Audrey directly challenged the opposition’s interpretation of the motion and responded to concerns about social pressure and affordability.

The recorded exchange showed a gap between “makeup benefits some men” and “men should wear makeup.” Examples involving actors or makeup artists support makeup in particular situations, but do not establish a general recommendation. The team’s speeches moved between professional necessity, personal choice and social encouragement without settling on a shared definition of “should.” A clear definition would help the team explain the scope of its claim and respond to the con side’s interpretation.

Several reasoning issues provide useful practice material. An example of wearing makeup to keep a job can reinforce an opponent’s concern about pressure, so the argument needs to explain why that example supports the pro case. Referring to appearance pressures on women does not, by itself, explain why extending those pressures to men would be fair. Presenting makeup and cosmetic procedures as essentially the only ways to improve appearance creates a false choice. Saying makeup artists can only practise on themselves is too absolute. Cultural examples also need clearer explanation of the connection between the practice, the tradition and the claim. The closing should answer the opposition’s central objection as well as summarize the team’s examples.

Coach Kai’s central position was that people have different needs, preferences and resources, so makeup should remain an individual choice. He accepted that makeup can improve appearance or serve professional purposes, then questioned whether those benefits justify a broader expectation. His responses addressed differing ideas of beauty, financial priorities, time and money costs, and the distinction between particular professional needs and expectations for men generally. His closing compared the cases and explained why those arguments mattered.

Reviewing the exchange also highlights precision in rebuttal. “Should” does not automatically mean “forced”; that interpretation needs justification, or the response should also address the motion as a recommendation. Professional examples are relevant but limited in scope. Claims about self-acceptance and health need qualification and support rather than blanket assertions. Declaring a point “invalid” does not establish that it has been defeated: explain which part fails and why. Ordinary examples of different priorities can make the reasoning clear without relying on an emotionally extreme scenario.

Suggested follow-up practice from the debate review is to agree on the meaning of the motion, connect each example to the central claim, and use the closing to explain why the case survives the opposition’s strongest objection. This guidance supplements the recorded classroom feedback; the assigned homework remains the ToC opening statement on students grading their teachers.

We began with an impromptu warm-up: “If we are bad at doing something, should we still do it?” Students chose a position and developed three reasons using “We should / shouldn’t, because… First… Second… Finally…” The focus was on forming their own ideas and supporting each point with an explanation or example.

We then explored the WCA competition topic: “Students should not be allowed to be on social media.” We discussed different arguments and viewed social-media examples to make the issues more concrete. Students considered the perspectives of students, parents, teachers, and social-media companies.

Arguments supporting restrictions included reduced sleep, copying dangerous activities, cheating, anxiety from comparison, unsafe online contact, inappropriate content, pressure to seek attention, and addictive use. Arguments against restrictions included opportunities to learn, access current information, maintain friendships, share experiences, find inspiration, connect with different communities, and support others.

After this discussion, each student spoke for approximately one minute and 30 seconds, presenting arguments, supporting points, and examples. Their responses became more thorough, and they approached the task more seriously. This was an initial exercise in developing independent arguments and entering a debate mindset; we have not yet covered detailed competition structures or techniques.

◆ Researchability: Can the student find information and evidence to develop it?

classContent:
◆ Eye practice at home: First, we briefly talked about eye control. Stare at a dot or one specific point for maybe two or three minutes every single day, or use two or three pictures to practise. This is especially useful for online competitions: the stronger your eye control, the more you can express with your eyes. The first practice is simply being able to keep your gaze on one specific point.

◆ Our speaking structure: Start with a situation you've noticed in your own life that connects to your topic. Use a rhetorical question: “Don't you find it kind of funny, weird or annoying when…?” Then ask: “How does it make you feel?” “Why does it make you feel this way?” And explain: “That's important because…” We want to take an observation, develop the feeling and reason behind it, and connect it to the topic you're speaking about.

◆ Why we practise this: It's a way to connect with the audience because it's relatable. When people recognize a common situation, they can think, “Yeah, I've noticed it too.” We often have common feelings about certain situations. That helps build credibility, helps build the connection, and helps you transfer some of that emotion to your audience. We want to be connected, relatable and authentic. Choose an observation listeners can recognize; a personal experience isn't automatically shared by everyone.

◆ Finding a topic you care about: In our discussion with Ariel, I asked her to think about things that matter to her—something she really cares about or finds frustrating. Swimming was a possible starting point: competitiveness, fairness, and technology that enhances a person's performance. What about clothing or other things people use? We talk about not using steroids or enhancers, yet people use sneakers, clothing and equipment that enhance their ability. Imagine swimming in clothes that reduce water drag, so you swim even faster. That gives us a question about fairness.

◆ Dig deeper: What is actual fair competition? Is it whatever you can do and however much money you can spend, with winning as the purpose? Or should ethics matter? You could then connect that ethical question to what AI can do. These were possible ideas to explore, not Ariel's confirmed new topic. I want students to think, “What do I care about?” rather than “I'm going to talk about a topic because it's a topic.”

◆ Follow-up plan: I said I would take a look at the speeches after class, since I didn't have another class afterwards. Hopefully I can edit or polish a speech a little, or give hints for what to do next time. This was my plan; completed script review and the availability of recordings or transcripts were not confirmed in these notes.

classContent:
Students began by presenting their homework on global warming and an imagined weather-changing device. Feedback focused on developing specific details, using clearer transitions, controlling gestures, and connecting with the audience. Sean joined as a new student and participated in the activities.

We briefly revisited the White House website and the game discussed previously, then moved into a new speaking prompt: a claim attributed to an AI company CEO that AI could destroy humanity by 2030. Students practised responding to this claim with their own reasoning. The claim served as a discussion prompt, rather than an established prediction.

The teacher demonstrated a three-minute response. Students then worked through two rounds of revision, applying earlier feedback to improve their speeches.

homework.title: What might the world look like in 2040?
steps:
Discussion statement: “Global warming and natural disasters will leave only 10% of the world habitable by 2040.”

Treat this as a claim to evaluate, rather than a confirmed fact. Habitable means suitable for people to live in.

◆ State your opinion: Explain whether you agree or disagree with the statement, and give reasons for your position.

◆ Create a hypothetical situation: Use “Imagine if…” to help the audience picture what the world could look like in 2040. Include specific details about the setting, people’s daily lives, and the effects of climate change or natural disasters.

◆ Develop your ideas: Explain the connections between your opinion and your imagined situation. Give enough detail for listeners to understand why your scenario matters.

◆ Write and rehearse: Aim for approximately 200–300 words. The main speaking target is at least three minutes, with two to three minutes as the practical range discussed in class. Time the speech aloud; the word count alone does not guarantee the speaking length. Add meaningful detail where needed.

◆ Prepare to present next class: Completing a written draft is only the first step. Students need to practise until they can deliver their ideas clearly in front of the class.

Materials: Bring pencils, pens, and a notebook. Student electronic devices will no longer be used in this class.

Starting next class, students should bring pencils, pens, and a notebook only. Student electronic devices will no longer be used in this class. This will help everyone focus on developing their own ideas, practising speaking, and listening respectfully to classmates.

classContent:
We began by reviewing the previous homework: responding to a hypothetical claim that, in a couple of decades, only 10% of Earth would remain habitable. Students needed to explain whether they thought this could happen, give their reasons, and describe what that future might look like from their perspective. The statement was a discussion prompt to evaluate, rather than an established prediction.

Students presented their responses and received feedback on preparation, organization, supporting details, speaking length, voice projection, confidence, and audience connection.

We then reviewed four characteristics of a strong speech topic:

◆ Societal impact: Why does the issue matter beyond the individual speaker?
◆ Personal connection: What experience, interest, or perspective connects the speaker to it?
◆ Researchability: Can the student find credible information and evidence to develop the speech?
◆ Uniqueness: What makes the topic or the speaker’s approach distinctive?

Using the FBI and police-officer example discussed in class, along with references to people in roles such as judges, we explored how personal experience can give a speaker credibility and a meaningful connection to an issue. Students considered how their own experiences could help explain why they care about a topic.

Each student proposed topics. We discussed their possibilities, narrowed or redirected ideas where needed, and began turning broad subjects into workable directions for a final speech.

homework.title: Develop the chosen speech topic

The work should begin to explain:

◆ What you want to discuss.
◆ Why it matters and how you connect to it.
◆ What information or examples you could use.
◆ What you want the audience to understand or take away.

This is development work for the final speech; it does not need to be a finished script yet. Bring the work so it can be reviewed and developed further.

Class materials: Bring a notebook and a pen or pencil. The previously established rule is that student electronic devices are not used in this class.

classContent:
◆ Class sequence: Students did not really remember their previous homework. We began with impromptu speeches, then moved into the recent roller-coaster situation discussed in the lesson and the question, “Why do we do things that are dangerous for us?”

◆ Roller-coaster worked example: The slide explored why people like roller coasters: the crazy feeling, speed and quick turns. People want to go again and again, and want faster and faster rides, because the experience is exciting and unique, and people may want to show off. The example then introduced a “however” contrast. Under a reference to Six Flags, the slide listed possible dangers: a ride breaking apart, tracks derailing, “brain problems,” broken bones, throwing up and dizziness. These were points in the classroom example, rather than a verified account of a particular accident or researched medical findings. The example asked: “Do you want more dangerous rides because they are fun, but also increase the chance you will get injured or die?” It ended with “What should we do?” and two unfinished “We should…” response lines.

◆ Speech outline: The second slide moved from the worked example to one situation students had seen or experienced. The questions were: Why? How does it affect the people involved or others? What can we do? The outline provided three numbered spaces for possible actions. This structure helps move a speech from describing a situation to explaining the reasons, effects and possible responses.

homework.title: Speech writing and rehearsal
steps: ◆ Homework: Write out the speech, then practise speaking it after preparing it. Use the outline for “Why do we do things that are dangerous for us?”: choose one situation you have seen or experienced; explain why people do it; explain how it affects the people involved or others; and explain what we can do. The general outline has three numbered spaces for possible actions. Use the roller-coaster worked example as a guide to developing the speech, rather than stopping at a list of ideas.

steps: Use the structure covered in class to prepare your response and write out the outline.
Connect with the audience through a rhetorical question or personal connection. Develop three main points, then end with your message: why is it important, and why should people care?

classContent:
◆ Homework presentations and preparation: Students presented their prepared material. We revisited the importance of preparing beforehand to organize logic and structure, reviewing and rehearsing until the material feels comfortable, then putting away the paper or computer when presenting so they can connect with the audience.

◆ Impromptu speech structures: The impromptu lesson focused on the five different types of questions that may appear in TOC and WSDA impromptu competitions. Students first tried answering questions before learning or understanding the structures. We then went over the structure, helped students understand the question types, and practised planning and delivering impromptu responses.

◆ Time management: Preparation and speaking share a combined seven minutes; students can decide how to divide that time. The speaking-time requirement in the practice was three minutes. The focus was to develop the answer sufficiently rather than finish too briefly.

◆ Connect, develop and finish: Connect with the audience through a rhetorical question or personal connection. Develop points 1, 2 and 3, then end with your message: why is it important, and why should people care? Write an outline, plan the response, and practise speaking from that preparation.

◆ Audience engagement and delivery: We worked on helping listeners understand the bigger picture through specific details and examples that they can visualize. Delivery should include vocal variation: energetic emphasis as well as more conversational moments. Emphasize important words and allow them enough time to stand out, rather than rushing through every word. Preparation should support direct eye contact and a more natural connection with the people in front of you.

◆ Later practice in this class: Jayden spoke first and needed to expand his short response. Nelson spoke second for three minutes and met the time requirement. Sean was called next. This was separate from the earlier homework presentations.

Today’s main focus was the four vocal tools: Power, Pitch, Pace, and Pause.

◆ Power refers to the strength and volume of the voice.
◆ Pitch is how high or low the voice sounds.
◆ Pace is the speed at which we speak.
◆ Pause means using purposeful silence to separate ideas and create emphasis.

The students explored how voice actors change their voices when playing characters in video games and cartoons. We examined how changes in voice, tone, pitch, and pace can make different characters sound unique.

We also reviewed the students’ previous speeches, provided individual feedback, and asked them to present again so that we could see who had memorized their speech and how naturally they could deliver it without relying on the paper.

During the dialogue activities, students practised playing different characters and tried to copy each character’s voice, tone, and hand gestures. They completed this through group practice, allowing them to explore how vocal and physical choices can make a character more believable.

We also completed warm-up exercises for the voice, self-awareness, and the body.

homework.title: Recorded homework
steps:
First priority: Students should spend their available practice time becoming more familiar with their final presentation. The goal is to get a clear grasp of the content so that the final delivery can become more natural and confident.

2. If additional time is available, students should practise the dialogues, focusing on how to present two different characters or roles through changes in voice, tone, and body language.

3. If time still remains, students can review the meaning and use of Power, Pitch, Pace, and Pause.

classContent:
We began with a short warm-up and an introduction to Original Oratory. We explored how a speech can examine cause and effect, impact, and solutions, helping students move from describing a topic toward explaining why it matters.

Each student delivered a self-introduction and received initial feedback on content and delivery. We focused on developing specific details, organizing ideas clearly, and becoming more aware of what happens while speaking.

A shared delivery priority was controlling filler words such as “uh” and “um.” We created an app to help students notice these sounds and increase their self-awareness. We discussed becoming comfortable with short pauses rather than immediately filling silence. We also worked on awareness of hand gestures and how purposeful movements can support a message.

Next, we explored topic selection through discussion of current events, including AI musicians and AI actors. Students brainstormed possible speech topics and considered five filters:

→ Personal connection: Does the topic connect to their experiences or interests?
→ Relatability: Can other people connect with it?
→ Uniqueness: Does it offer a distinctive perspective?
→ Societal impact: Why does it matter to people or communities?
→ Researchability: Can they find credible information and specific examples?

We then began identifying a claim or central idea within each topic: what the student thinks about it and what they want the audience to understand.

homework.title: Assigned homework
steps:
Prepare approximately 200 words based on your chosen topic. Explain your thoughts and opinions, and begin developing the claim or central idea you could use in your speech.

Be ready to present this at the beginning of the next class. Students may use their notes while presenting if needed. Practising aloud beforehand will help them become familiar with their ideas and notice where they need to pause.

classContent:
Today’s main focus was speaking with the audience, rather than simply talking at them. The class generally showed good structure and logic, so we introduced audience-engagement techniques: rhetorical questions, direct audience address, visualization, sensory language, and emotional expression.

We also discussed improving clarity by simplifying complex explanations and shortening sentences when ideas were difficult to express or follow.

We reviewed opening, body, and conclusion, explored different hooks, and developed the cause → effect → impact → solution framework. Examples from world-champion speeches and NSDA Original Oratory speakers helped illustrate the different parts.

The central goal was to identify a problem in society, explain why it matters, raise awareness, and offer a potential solution. Students should express their own stance and viewpoint, rather than only introduce information about a topic.

Overall, the teacher was very pleased with the class. Everyone listened attentively, worked well and thought deeply about what they needed to complete. The students showed motivation and a positive attitude, and appeared to enjoy the lesson. Several students had also done research, which the teacher wanted to acknowledge and applaud.

Use the form prompts: opening hooks; main thesis, social problem and relevance; signposting; cause; effect; impact; personal connection; bridge towards hope and solution; call to action; reverse hook.

classContent:
◆ Homework review and audience engagement

We began by reviewing the students’ homework speeches. One shared priority was maintaining audience engagement throughout the speech. We discussed using rhetorical questions beyond the opening to reconnect with listeners as the ideas develop.

◆ Rhetorical devices and persuasion

We explored commonly used rhetorical devices: anaphora, parallelism, juxtaposition, hyperbole, simile, metaphor and the rule of three. These techniques can help emphasize key ideas and make the language more memorable. We also briefly introduced ethos, pathos and logos.

◆ Personal connection and storytelling

The main focus was developing a stronger personal connection: explaining why the speaker cares about the issue and connecting that experience to the wider message. We explored the hero’s journey and practised planning a personal narrative using this sequence:

Background → Struggle → Lowest point → Words of wisdom → Apply → Success

Students began developing their personal connection for inclusion in their speeches. Some said they had completed writing at home but had not brought their scripts. With the final presentation approaching, I need to review each complete script and provide basic polishing. Today’s central task was adding the personal connection and strengthening the language through commonly used rhetorical devices.

homework.title: Completed speech script

classContent:
We worked on power, pitch, pace, and pauses; emotional expression; and 20 hand gestures. Students reviewed their speeches and practised memorization techniques:

1. Read the speech aloud 10 times.
2. Record it.
3. Listen to the recording and visualize the speech.
4. Practise with exaggerated emotions.
5. Practise with hand gestures.
6. Practise in a presentation setting.

I also demonstrated how I memorize my own competition speeches. Students then completed peer editing and gave one another feedback.

classContent:
We began with a body warm-up, including jumping and moving left and right, to help students relax and get their blood pumping. We then warmed up their voices through tongue twisters, articulation exercises, and practice with emotional facial expressions.

Next, we introduced a structure for self-introductions and practised using it. Mia gave several self-introductions of approximately one minute each, while Charlotte gave one and appeared more hesitant.

Our topic discussion focused on SDG 6: Clean Water and Sanitation. We explored the problems affecting clean water, what makes water dirty, methods currently used to clean it, and pollution around the world. This led to a discussion about why we need to protect our clean water sources.

We also introduced self-awareness when presenting, focusing on eye contact, hands, feet, and voice. Students were encouraged to take individual speaking turns, although they continued to prefer coming up together. Mia sometimes encouraged Charlotte to go first, while Charlotte appeared particularly nervous about speaking alone.

Finally, we watched an NSDA storytelling speech, Dinosaur Went to Class. This provided a more accessible example to discuss, as some adult championship speeches could be difficult for them to understand.

The focus of the first one or two days is to help students become more comfortable speaking aloud and gradually overcome their fear of presenting as we explore more topics.

classContent:
We began with a self-awareness warm-up, finding differences between two pictures. This helped students practise noticing details about themselves and their surroundings—an important foundation for becoming aware of their voice, movements, and audience while speaking.

We then began a body warm-up but stopped it early when students started bumping into desks, to keep the activity safe.

Charlotte took an independent speaking turn, with Mia nearby. We introduced clapping once for each word in a short sentence to help her notice and slow her speaking pace. The teacher demonstrated this with a simple sentence such as “I really like blueberries.” The practice suggestion was to repeat the sentence at the same steady pace without clapping.

The teacher also proposed using a music stand to hold the script, freeing both hands for gestures and making it easier to practise speaking directly to the audience. This is a proposed classroom support, not an assigned homework task.

Both students continued practising their speeches. Mia spoke at a more comfortable pace and began using her free hand to gesture while speaking.

We then added hand gestures to the speech practice. The teacher recorded a demonstration video showing how to follow the gestures, giving students a clear model to use during rehearsal.

Our second speech topic was poverty. We explored what poverty means, why it is a problem around the world, and other issues connected with it. We watched examples of places where poverty is prevalent and reviewed the basic speech structure: opening, body, and conclusion.

We also practised organizing ideas around problems and solutions. Students considered different problems and thought about possible ways to solve them. Finally, we introduced simple impromptu questions so they could practise forming an answer and responding more quickly.

classContent:
◆ Homework review and preparation

We began by reviewing homework. Both students reported practising their speech once or twice. We discussed practising more regularly as we begin preparing for the final presentation.

◆ Infrastructure and key messages

Today’s topic was infrastructure. Although the concept was challenging, we introduced it through familiar examples: roads, lighting, pipes and bridges—the systems and structures that help places function. We kept the discussion concrete rather than exploring infrastructure problems around the world in depth, to keep the introduction suitable for their age.

We also introduced the idea of a key message, using advertisements to show how a clear central idea can be obvious, easy to understand and easy to remember.

◆ Developing the final speeches

The students completed a planning activity and chose favourite sports as their subject. Mia chose swimming. Charlotte initially chose basketball before changing to swimming, so both final speeches are now about swimming. We worked on giving the speeches different angles. I helped polish and expand their drafts.

From previous summer, winter and other camps, I have found that starting final-speech preparation two days in advance gives students a better chance of memorizing their speech. We are beginning preparation early so they can read aloud, become comfortable with the wording and work towards presenting without looking at paper.

◆ Planned next lesson

Once they are more familiar with the wording, we plan to work on voice, vocal variety and body language tomorrow, alongside our last topic before the final presentation.

homework.title: Final swimming speech practice

Focus on becoming comfortable with the words and saying the sentences clearly.
Gradually become less dependent on the script, working towards delivering the final presentation without looking at paper.

classContent:
◆ Homework presentations and concentration

We began with presentations of the homework speeches. Both Mia and Charlotte came on stage confidently and used hand gestures during their first attempt.

On the second attempt, we introduced distractions so they could practise maintaining concentration while speaking. Both managed reasonably well, although neither particularly enjoyed the distractions. Charlotte’s pace became a little fast during this attempt.

◆ Vocal variety and body language

Today’s main focus was vocal variety and body language. We started with articulation practice, then explored power, pitch, pace and pause. We worked through the Bear and the Bee dialogue and looked at examples of voice actors, particularly in video games, demonstrating how they change their voices. We did not introduce the different categories of dialogue today.
